messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar Khalil, a 37-year-old married firefighter from a Middle Eastern family, came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed around one terrifying period in which he had been stalked. The stalking had begun with small, unsettling details he could not dismiss: a bicycle left repeatedly outside his station and later near his home, a shadowy figure seeming to appear at the edge of streets he used on his commute, and the sickening sense that he was being followed or tracked even when he tried to tell himself he was overreacting. What made the experience especially potent was that it invaded the ordinary spaces of his day—driving to work, walking into a building, stepping outside after a shift—so that physical locations no longer felt neutral. During the most frightening stretches, Omar would enter a room and immediately scan for exits, and he became intensely alert to unexpected or loud sounds, because each abrupt noise felt to him like the start of something he had to prepare for.

As the stalking continued, those triggers began pulling the event back into him with little warning. Seeing a bicycle locked near the firehouse, passing a familiar intersection, or noticing a car pacing him on the road could instantly bring the full memory back, not as a distant recollection but as a rush that made him stop what he was doing. He described how the memory would arrive in pieces he could not hold onto for long: he knew what had happened, yet when he tried to explain it he found himself unable to find the words, and the emotion rose so quickly that he had to break off and sit in silence. Each return of the memory seemed to confirm what he had already started to believe about himself. Omar had come to think that he had permanently changed for the worse, that the fear and jumpiness meant he was going crazy, and that his inability to handle the situation showed he was weak in a way he had never allowed himself to be before. The more the memory broke through, the more it fed those beliefs, and the more ashamed and altered he felt.

Those appraisals quickly spread into the way he moved through the world. Believing that he had been weakened and was no longer trustworthy in his own judgment, Omar became even more on guard. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, especially when he was off duty or alone, and the moment he entered any room or building his eyes went to doors, hallways, and exits. Because he was convinced that danger could appear without warning and that he was no longer the man he had been, he began treating ordinary places as if they were potential traps. A quiet restaurant, the grocery store, the parking lot outside his station, even the gym near his home all became settings where he felt the need to check who was behind him and whether someone might be tracking his route. He avoided certain streets and found himself making detours that lengthened his commute, and after a while the bicycle itself—once merely a detail in the stalking—became enough to set his whole body on edge.

What frightened Omar most was how the threat state seemed to keep his mind tied to the event. An unexpected bang in the station, a slammed locker door, or footsteps too close behind him would send him back to the same conviction that he was under watch and had to stay ready. That vigilance, in turn, made him think even more harshly about himself: if he had to keep scanning, if he could never relax, then something in him must be fundamentally damaged. On the worst days, the memory would surface while he was already alert, and the combination left him feeling overwhelmed and exposed, as though he were failing at the very job that depended on steadiness. Over weeks and months, this fed a tightening cycle in which every sign of being followed or every sharp sound confirmed his fear, and every confirmation deepened his sense of permanent change and weakness. He withdrew from colleagues, stopped lingering after shifts, and became wary even in the company of other people because he could not shake the sense that someone might mean him harm.

By the time he sought help, Omar was exhausted by living this way and frightened by how small his world had become. He said he wanted to keep protecting his family and doing his work, but he was most afraid that if he continued alone he would either break down completely or remain trapped in this state of watching, checking, and reliving.
